Despite being insulted by the recent American decision to maintain an embargo on Cuba, President Rafael Cortez gave a speech earlier today regarding American use of Guantanamo Bay, a 45-square mile plot of land administrated by the United States on the southern coast of Cuba. The land contains a naval base, a detention center, and a small city dedicated to civilian contractors and service personnel. In accordance with the Cuban-American Treaty of 1903, Cuba has, in the president’s words, been “coerced and bullied” into leasing the land to the United States. Only one check from the lease has been cashed since the 1959 revolution in Cuba, and Fidel Castro insisted it was an accident.

Like his predecessors, the president criticized U.S. control of the land, stating that it was forcibly extracted from Cuba during American occupation of the island after the Spanish-American War. He pointed out that, according to the treaty, Guantanamo Bay was supposed to be used only for a coaling station, not a full-fledged modern naval base or a detention center for terrorists.

President Cortez went as far as to call the U.S. government hypocritical for condemning human rights violations in Cuba while defending the existence of the Guantanamo detention center, where stories of torture and denial of human rights abound. However, despite his harsh words, the president said he wants to create a new agreement that would void the Cuban-American Treaty of 1903 while allowing the Americans to retain their naval base and detention center if they so choose.

A preliminary draft of a potential agreement, written by the Cuban legislature by request of the president, includes the following:

  • The Guantanamo Bay area will be split in two sections: one half contains unused land within American jurisdiction that will be fully returned to Cuba, and one half contains the American naval base, administrative outpost, and detention center, which will continue to be administered by the United States.
  • Cuba will cash a collection of uncashed lease checks from 1959 to 2022 for a sum of $257,355, and it will accept future checks.
  • The annual lease paid to Cuba by the United States will remain at $4,085 USD.
  • Construction of a bridge across Guantanamo Bay will be considered in order to make transportation between the American regions easier.
  • The new agreement would extend to January 1st, 2040, at which point both nations must agree on a revision or renewal of the contract by January 1st, 2041.

Guantanamo Bay and the embargo represent the two biggest hurdles Cuba and the United States must overcome in order to normalize relations, and with the embargo still in place for the time being, President Cortez hopes the U.S. will agree to resolve at least one of the two issues. If not, relations between the nations will stagnate and deteriorate.
